entities.name: Stig Andersen Hvide
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Stig Andersen Hvide, a formidable Danish magnate and marshal (Marsk), emerged as the preeminent leader of the outlaws following the assassination of King Eric V "Klipping" of Denmark on November 22, 1286. His life, culminating in his death in 1293, is inextricably linked to one of medieval Denmark's most dramatic political upheavals, casting him as both a regicide and a figure of popular resistance in the collective memory of the Scandinavian region. His actions profoundly challenged the nascent consolidation of royal power in 13th-century Denmark, shaping the political landscape for decades.

After King Eric V was murdered in the barn of Finderup, Stig Andersen Hvide, along with eight other noblemen, was accused and outlawed by the Danehof (parliament) held in Nyborg in 1287. Despite the lack of definitive proof, the swift condemnation by the regency government, led by Queen Dowager Agnes and Erik VI Menved, forced Stig and his confederates into exile. From their stronghold on the island of Hjelm in the Kattegat, and with support from King Eric VI of Norway, they launched a series of raids against Danish coastal towns and royal lands, effectively maintaining a state of civil unrest and challenging the authority of the Danish crown. These actions included the sacking of Copenhagen in 1289, demonstrating their continued potency as a political and military force.

The outlawry of Marsk Stig and his subsequent maritime warfare against Denmark had lasting consequences for the balance of power between the Danish monarchy and its powerful nobility, contributing to a period of royal weakness and noble ascendancy. His defiance became a potent symbol of resistance against perceived royal tyranny, echoing through subsequent generations. While historical records remain ambiguous about his direct involvement in the regicide, his leadership of the outlawed faction cemented his place in Danish history as a pivotal figure in the struggle between crown and aristocracy.
